item.title: Uber to Pay $40 Million to Parents of Woman Fatally Hit by Car
item.description:
Uber Technologies Inc. has been ordered to pay $40 million to the parents of a woman who was fatally struck by a vehicle after a driver left her and a friend on a California freeway, an arbitration document and lawyer said.

On Aug. 12, 2023, the woman, Emily Normandin-Parker, 23, and her friend Luna Moore called an Uber to drive them home after a night out in Orange County, Calif., the document said. After Ms. Moore became sick and vomited, the driver, Vu Tran, pulled over on State Route 73 and stopped at a gore point, it said, referring to the triangular plot of land where a road forks at an intersection or ramp.

While stopped in an “unsafe and illegal” spot, Mr. Tran argued with Ms. Moore about a cleaning fee, the document said. He showed “no concern for Normandin-Parker’s whereabouts despite knowing she had exited the vehicle and was intoxicated,” it said.

Ms. Normandin-Moore wandered into traffic “in an inebriated state” and was struck and killed by a vehicle that was traveling 70 miles per hour, the arbitration document said.

The award was announced as the outcome of arbitration process conducted in March by Richard A. Stone, an arbitrator and retired judge, in Los Angeles. It touched on the legal extent to which Uber is responsible for the actions of its drivers, an issue that has arisen in other lawsuits.

The arbitration document was published on Thursday by the lawyers representing Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents, Carol Normandin and Ken Parker.

The parents and Ms. Moore accused Mr. Tran and Uber of negligence, asserting that the company had liability as a common carrier. That classification applies to companies that provide transportation services to the public, obligating them to protect and warn passengers of any dangers.

Uber argued that, under California Proposition 22, Uber and Lyft drivers are classified as independent contractors and that the company merely “provides a software platform connecting riders with independent third-party drivers,” the document said.

But the arbitrator noted that Uber controlled key aspects of the rider experience, set fares and profited directly from rides. Uber, he found, was “vicariously liable” for Mr. Tran’s negligence because it had a duty for safety that cannot be delegated.

Ms. Moore also presented claims of intentional infliction of emotional distress against Mr. Tran.

Mr. Tran testified that he picked up the women from a bar early that Saturday morning and knew that they were inebriated, but not to what extent, according to the arbitration document. After Ms. Moore became sick and the women were told to leave the car, Mr. Tran testified that he called Uber within minutes and asked that Ms. Moore be charged a cleaning fee.

That demonstrated that Mr. Tran had a “single-minded fixation” on the state of his car and a lack of interest in the riders’ safety, the judge found.

Ms. Moore was awarded $300,000, the decision said.

Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents “suffered immense loss” and were each awarded $20 million, the document said.

Lawyers for the family said in a statement that Uber had tried to keep the outcome of the arbitration and award confidential by proposing a settlement agreement that would have required the parents to pay a $10 million penalty for each time they discussed it publicly. The parents turned it down.

“You cannot claim to put safety first while fighting to silence the families whose lives have been devastated when that promise is broken,” the statement said.

Uber said it “ultimately did not pursue confidentiality” in the case.

The decision “makes clear that companies advertising safety cannot walk away from the responsibility that comes with those promises,” Rahul Ravipudi, one of the lawyers representing Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents, said in the law firm’s statement.

In an emailed statement on Friday, Uber said that the driver no longer had access to the app, but that he had completed nearly 6,000 trips with a 4.96 rating, and “not a single incident involved unsafe drop-offs, freeway stops or rider injury.”

The company said that it was strengthening its approach to safety with new technology, policies and safeguards, including additional guidance to drivers about avoiding drop-offs in unsafe locations.

“While we respect the arbitration process, we believe the arbitrator was wrong in holding Uber legally responsible for the tragic events of that night,” it said.

item.title: 5 Takeaways From Ari Emanuel’s Memoir
item.description:
Ari Emanuel, the hard-charging, expletive-hurling Hollywood agent who inspired the character of Ari Gold on the HBO show “Entourage,” has written a memoir that breathlessly charges through its 400-plus pages, dropping names, settling scores and swearing up a storm.

“Roll the Calls” unapologetically burnishes the persona Mr. Emanuel has cultivated as a rage-fueled brawler who will go to the mat for his clients. It chronicles his rise to becoming one of the richest and most powerful men in sports and entertainment, whose companies own the WME talent agency, World Wrestling Entertainment, Ultimate Fighting Championship, Broadway theaters and the Frieze art fairs.

But the memoir is also the story of a middle-class kid from Chicago who struggled with dyslexia in a family of overachievers and who, even now, is never satisfied with what he has achieved. “The highs never last,” he writes. “No matter how high, they just never last.”

Many boldface names appear in “Roll the Calls,” which was written with J.R. Moehringer (the ghostwriter for Prince Harry’s “Spare”). Mr. Emanuel writes about signing Oprah Winfrey (“tears in my eyes”), contradicting President Obama for his take on the future of streaming and letting Donald Trump go as a client when he first took office.

“I tell him I’ve never dropped a client with such ease,” Mr. Emanuel writes. “And I tell him I didn’t vote for him.”

Here are some of the takeaways from the book, which Alfred A. Knopf will release on Tuesday.

One of Mr. Emanuel’s favorite punching bags is Jeffrey Katzenberg, the former Disney and DreamWorks executive who is also a major political fund raiser. In Mr. Emanuel’s telling, Mr. Katzenberg refused to pay Mr. Emanuel’s agency for putting together the stars and creative team for the CBS sitcom “Ink.” And he had the nerve to buy Los Angeles Lakers floor seats out from under Mr. Emanuel. (Mr. Emanuel threatened to sue Mr. Katzenberg over those tickets.) Mr. Emanuel also blames Mr. Katzenberg for President Trump’s re-election. According to Mr. Emanuel, it was Mr. Katzenberg, as President Biden’s top donor, who orchestrated “all the obfuscation about Biden’s obvious mental impairment.”

Mr. Berg, the director of movies including “Friday Night Lights” who has been a friend of Mr. Emanuel’s since college, has always been his client. When Mr. Berg was offered the opportunity to direct “American Beauty,” Mr. Emanuel said he warned him: When you meet the DreamWorks executives, don’t mention that you want your girlfriend to star. The meeting, with Steven Spielberg, David Geffen and Mr. Katzenberg, went well until they asked Mr. Berg if he had any casting suggestions. Mr. Berg said his girlfriend — Madonna — would be perfect. The three leaned back. He did not get the gig. Sam Mendes ultimately won the job — and the Oscar for best director.

He carps about the $7 billion valuation for CAA, WME’s closest rival (“a helluva lot more than us, even though we’re more profitable — and bigger”) and criticizes that agency for not condemning Kanye West after one of his anti-Semitic tirades. But he never once mentions the agency’s chief executive, Bryan Lourd, by name. Also omitted is David Ellison, even though Mr. Ellison has been advising Mr. Emanuel on his acquisition of Warner Bros. None of today’s studio heads make appearances, either.

Mr. Emanuel prides himself on standing up for what he thinks is right. After the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi was murdered in Istanbul by Saudi operatives in 2018, Mr. Emanuel returned a $400 million investment from Saudi Arabia’s government investment fund. And in 2024, while being honored by the Simon Wiesenthal Center, a Jewish human rights organization, he condemned Israel’s conservative prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, calling him an “agent of chaos, hatred, division and destruction.” Despite Mr. Emanuel’s liberal politics, though, he doesn’t delve into any differences he may have with President Trump, beyond dropping him as a client, or with Mr. Emanuel’s right-leaning pals Elon Musk and Dana White, the U.F.C. chief executive. “I can’t fight anymore,” Mr. Emanuel writes. “I can’t have beef with half my friends. I can’t hate half my country.”

Mr. Emanuel’s morning routine involves waking up at 4 a.m., stretching for 40 minutes and then doing breath work, sauna, meditation, an ice plunge and infrared light therapy before ingesting a protein shake and a cup of live worms to fight off “the bad bacteria in my gut.” He describes a recent lunch with his old CAA boss, Michael Ovitz. Mr. Emanuel writes: “He goes to the gym; he thinks that means he’s taking care of himself. But it doesn’t. I scold him. He hasn’t gotten his blood work done in years, he isn’t doing ice plunges, he isn’t doing daily breath work, he isn’t fasting. And he needs to be eating worms.”

item.title: U.S. and China Discuss System to Warn of A.I. National Security Issues
item.description:
The United States and China discussed on Sunday the creation of a notification system that would allow the countries to alert each other about national security issues related to artificial intelligence.

The countries spoke about the need for such a mechanism during a day of economic talks involving Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent; Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative; and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng. The meetings took place in New York ahead of President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington later this week, and they were intended to lay the groundwork for potential agreements between the world’s two largest economies on artificial intelligence, trade and the war in Iran.

The idea a new mechanism for addressing A.I. underscores the growing concern around the world that the rapidly evolving technology could pose national security risks.

Speaking after the meetings, which were held at the New York offices of JPMorgan Chase, Mr. Bessent said that the mechanism would be called “the U.S.-China A.I. dialogue” and that it would aim to ensure that the two countries had a shared vision on the goals of A.I. and threats that it poses.

Explaining that the notification system would be activated when a matter related to A.I. reaches the national security level, Mr. Bessent added: “We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 A.I. powers in the world is very important.”

The United States and China have been racing to become the dominant powers in artificial intelligence technology at a time when there is increasing demand to regulate the industry because of concerns that it could spiral out of human control and be used for hacking and the development of lethal weapons.

America’s leading A.I. companies have recently published reports disclosing that their models have breached or bypassed contained testing environments. U.S. officials are also concerned about the potential for A.I. to enhance Chinese hacking operations, military capabilities and surveillance systems.

In a report earlier this month, the Trump administration accused Chinese companies of taking proprietary functions and capabilities from American A.I. models in an “aggressive, malicious and targeted” way. The issue is expected to be a topic of discussion between President Trump and Mr. Xi when they meet.

Mr. Bessent and Mr. Greer also said that they discussed trade with their Chinese counterparts. U.S. officials said they were moving forward with setting up a new so-called Board of Trade, a concept they introduced earlier this year, which would promote trade in nonsensitive goods between the United States and China.

The goods would include Chinese-made consumer goods and low-tech items, as well as American energy products, agricultural goods and potentially medical devices, Mr. Greer said.

Government officials on both sides were continuing to work, Mr. Greer said, to find a critical mass of goods that could be “traded in a balanced way, and create a kind of ballast for the relationship.”

The United States and China agreed to a one-year trade truce last October after engaging in a tit-for-tat war of tariffs and export controls that destabilized the global economy for months.
